turns.title: Write-through flashcard

Write-through
Every write goes to cache and main memory immediately, so memory is always up to date.

turns.title: Write-policy flashcard set
turns.html:
Write-through
Write cache and memory immediately; memory always current.
Write-back
Write cache only; mark dirty; flush to memory on eviction.
Write-allocate
On a write miss, load the block into cache, then write there.
No-write-allocate
On a write miss, write straight to memory and skip the cache.

Write-allocate

No-write-allocate
On a write miss, write straight to memory and skip the cache.
Write-combining
Batch small writes in a buffer, then flush them together as one burst.

conversations.topic: Building and refining a JavaScript framework glossary widget

turns.html:
JavaScript Framework Glossary

  • Component — Reusable UI building block with its own logic and style.
  • Props — Inputs passed from a parent to a child component.
  • State — Internal data that changes over time and triggers re-renders.
  • Virtual DOM — In-memory representation of the real DOM, used for efficient diffing.
  • Hooks — Functions that let you use state and lifecycle features in function components.
  • Reactive — Automatically updating UI when underlying data changes.
  • Directive — Special attribute in templates that applies behavior to the DOM.
  • SSR — Server-Side Rendering: generating HTML on the server for faster first paint.

turns.html:
Golden Shrimp Pasta

Prep 10 min Cook 15 min Serves 2
  • 200g linguine
  • 250g shrimp, peeled
  • 3 cloves garlic, minced
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 1/4 tsp chili flakes
  • 1/2 cup white wine
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 1 lemon (zest + juice)
  • 2 tbsp parsley, chopped
  • Salt and pepper
  1. Boil pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1/2 cup pasta water.
  2. Heat olive oil in a pan, sauté garlic and chili flakes for 30 seconds.
  3. Add shrimp, cook until pink, about 2 minutes per side. Remove and set aside.
  4. Pour in wine, simmer 2 minutes. Stir in butter and lemon juice.
  5. Return shrimp, add pasta and a splash of pasta water. Toss to coat.
  6. Finish with lemon zest, parsley, salt and pepper. Serve hot.

conversations.topic: Calculating and visualizing a team's sprint velocity with a formula and steps.

turns.html:
Sprint Velocity Formula

velocity = total_story_points / number_of_sprints

Use the last 3–6 sprints for a stable number. Don't count partially completed work.

Steps

  1. Pick the last 5 sprints.
  2. Total the story points completed in each.
  3. Divide by 5.
  4. Round to the nearest whole point.
Example: 22 + 19 + 25 + 21 + 23 = 110; 110 ÷ 5 = 22.

Brewery Glossary
ABV

Alcohol by volume — how strong the beer is. A 12 oz pour at 5% ABV contains roughly 0.6 oz of pure alcohol.

IBU

International Bitterness Units — a 0–100 scale. Light lagers sit near 10, aggressive IPAs push past 70.

SRM

Standard Reference Method — a color number. 2 is pale straw, 40 is opaque black. Not related to flavor intensity.

Dry-hopped

Hops added after fermentation instead of during the boil. Adds aroma without adding much bitterness.

conversations.topic: recipe_card

turns.html:
Garlic Butter Shrimp Pasta

Prep 10 min Cook 15 min Serves 4

Ingredients

  • 400g linguine
  • 500g large shrimp, peeled
  • 4 tbsp butter
  • 6 cloves garlic, minced
  • 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
  • 1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
  • 1 lemon, juiced and zested
  • Salt and black pepper to taste
  • Parmesan cheese for serving

Steps

  1. Boil pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1/2 cup pasta water.
  2. Melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and red pepper flakes; cook 1 minute.
  3. Add shrimp; cook 2-3 minutes per side until pink. Remove shrimp and set aside.
  4. Add pasta, lemon juice, zest, and pasta water to skillet. Toss to coat.
  5. Return shrimp, add parsley, season with salt and pepper. Serve with Parmesan.

turns.html:
HTML cheat sheet

Tap a tag to read a bit more about it.

<h1> — Top-level heading

Use exactly one per page for the main title. Browsers style it large and bold by default.

<a> — Hyperlink

The href attribute points at the destination. Add target="_blank" to open in a new tab.

<img> — Embed an image

Self-closing tag. Requires src and an alt description for accessibility.

<form> — Input group

Wraps controls like <input> and submits values to a server via its action.

<button> — Action

Keyboard-focusable by default. Use type="button" unless it should submit a form.

turns.html:
Weeknight Dal

Prep 10 min Cook 25 min Serves 4

Ingredients

  • 1 cup red lentils
  • 3 cups water
  • 1 can diced tomatoes
  • 1 onion, diced
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • 1 inch ginger, grated
  • 1 tsp cumin
  • 1 tsp turmeric
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 2 tbsp oil
  • Cilantro for garnish

Steps

  1. Rinse lentils until water runs clear.
  2. Sauté onion in oil until golden, add garlic and ginger, cook 1 min.
  3. Add spices, stir 30 seconds, then add tomatoes and cook 2 min.
  4. Add lentils and water, bring to boil, simmer 20 min until soft.
  5. Season with salt, garnish with cilantro, serve with rice.

HTTP Status Codes Grouped by Type
Success (2xx)
  • 200 OK – Standard success response.
  • 201 Created – Resource created.
  • 204 No Content – Success with no body.
Redirects (3xx)
  • 301 Moved Permanently – Permanent redirect.
  • 302 Found – Temporary redirect.
  • 304 Not Modified – Cached version is current.
Client Errors (4xx)
  • 400 Bad Request – Malformed request.
  • 401 Unauthorized – Authentication required.
  • 403 Forbidden – Server refuses to authorize.
  • 404 Not Found – Resource doesn't exist.
Server Errors (5xx)
  • 500 Internal Server Error – Generic server error.
  • 502 Bad Gateway – Invalid response from upstream.
  • 503 Service Unavailable – Server overloaded or down.

turns.html:
Photography exposure glossary

  • Aperture — lens opening size; f/1.8 is wide, f/16 is narrow.
  • Shutter speed — how long the sensor is exposed, e.g. 1/500s freezes motion.
  • ISO — sensor sensitivity to light; higher ISO brightens but adds noise.
  • EV — exposure value; +1 EV doubles the light, −1 halves it.

turns.html:
Meal-prep lasagna cups

Prep 20 minServes 4Bake 25 min
  • 12 lasagna noodles, cooked
  • 2 cups ricotta
  • 1 egg
  • 2 cups marinara
  • 1 cup mozzarella, shredded
  • ¼ cup parmesan, grated
  • 1 tsp Italian seasoning
  • Salt and pepper to taste
  1. Preheat oven to 375°F. Grease a 12-cup muffin tin.
  2. Mix ricotta, egg, parmesan, Italian seasoning, salt, and pepper in a bowl.
  3. Cut each lasagna noodle into 3 strips. Press 2–3 strips into each muffin cup to form a cup shape.
  4. Spoon 1 tbsp ricotta mixture into each cup, then 1 tbsp marinara. Repeat layers until cups are full.
  5. Top each with mozzarella. Bake 22–25 min until bubbly and golden.
  6. Cool 5 min before removing. Store refrigerated up to 4 days.

turns.html:
Creamy Tomato Pasta

Serves 2 · 25 min · Vegetarian

Ingredients
  • 200 g pasta (penne or rigatoni)
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 3 cloves garlic, sliced
  • 400 g canned crushed tomatoes
  • 60 ml heavy cream
  • 1 tsp dried oregano
  • Salt and black pepper, to taste
  • Fresh basil leaves, to garnish
Steps
  1. Boil pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 120 ml pasta water.
  2. Warm olive oil in a pan, add garlic, cook 1 min until fragrant.
  3. Add crushed tomatoes and oregano. Simmer 8 min, stirring.
  4. Stir in cream and a splash of pasta water to loosen.
  5. Add drained pasta, toss to coat. Season with salt and pepper.
  6. Serve topped with torn basil.

Common questions about the 7-day plan.

Workouts this week
5 sessions
Rest days
2 days
balanced
Do I need a gym membership?
No — every session uses bodyweight or a pair of dumbbells. The plan is designed for a living-room floor space of about 2×2 metres.
What if I miss a day?
Just shift the remaining sessions forward. The week resets on Monday; you don't need to double up.
How long is each workout?
Between 20 and 35 minutes, including a 4-minute warm-up and a 3-minute cool-down.
Can I swap rest days?
Yes. Keep at least one rest day between two strength sessions. If you move Wednesday's rest to Thursday, push Thursday's session to Friday.
Is there a warm-up?
Every session starts with the same 4-minute routine: 40s march, 40s arm circles, 40s hip hinges, 40s easy squats, then 2×20s of your choice.

conversations.topic: Building and refining a bread baking glossary widget

turns.html:
Bread Baking Glossary

  • Autolyse — Resting flour and water before salt or yeast so the flour hydrates and gluten begins forming on its own.
  • Hydration — Water weight as a share of flour weight. 75% means 750 g water to 1000 g flour.
  • Bulk ferment — The first rise of the whole dough, before shaping.
  • Proof — The final rise of shaped loaves, usually in a basket or tin.
  • Levain — A build of ripe starter used to raise a specific dough.
  • Windowpane — Stretching dough thin enough to see light through; the sign gluten is developed.

turns.html:
Seed-Sowing FAQ

Zone 7a · last frost April 15

When do I start tomatoes indoors?

Six to eight weeks before last frost — around late February. Sow 1/4 in deep at 75 °F.

Can I direct-sow carrots in March?

Yes, if soil is workable and above 40 °F. Thin to 2 in apart once tops reach 2 in.

How often should I water seedlings?

Keep the top inch moist, not soggy. Bottom-water twice a week is usually enough indoors.

conversations.topic: Bike commute time dashboard — formula, steps, then refine into filtering, chart types, unit switching, and a checklist.

turns.html:
Bike Commute Time

A small dashboard that computes your typical door-to-door pedal time from distance and speed, with a breakdown of the moving parts. All numbers assume a 10 km round trip at 18 km/h plus 6 minutes of stops and locks.

commute = distance / speed * 60 + stops + locks
Distance10km
Speed18km/h
Ride time33min
Total commute43min
  1. Measure one-way distance and double it.
  2. Divide distance by your average speed, then multiply by 60 for minutes.
  3. Add stop time (lights, detours) and lock time at each end.

Ride time: 10 / 18 × 60 = 33.3 min → 33 min. Total: 33 + 6 + 4 = 43 min.

conversations.topic: Interactive lemonade recipe card with scaling, variations, and a flavor dashboard

turns.html:
Classic Lemonade

Prep 10 minServes 4
  • 1 cup fresh lemon juice (about 4–6 lemons)
  • 1 cup granulated sugar
  • 4 cups cold water
  • Ice, for serving
  • Lemon slices, for garnish
  1. Juice the lemons and strain out seeds.
  2. In a small saucepan, combine sugar and 1 cup water. Warm over low heat until sugar dissolves. Let cool.
  3. In a large pitcher, combine lemon juice, sugar syrup, and remaining 3 cups water.
  4. Stir well, taste, and adjust sweetness if needed.
  5. Serve over ice with lemon slices.

turns.html:
Scaled Lemonade

Adjust the slider or use the buttons to scale the recipe.

Scale:1.5x
  • 1½ cups fresh lemon juice (about 6–9 lemons)
  • 1½ cups granulated sugar
  • 6 cups cold water
  • Ice, for serving
  • Lemon slices, for garnish
  1. Juice the lemons and strain out seeds.
  2. In a small saucepan, combine sugar and 1½ cups water. Warm over low heat until sugar dissolves. Let cool.
  3. In a large pitcher, combine lemon juice, sugar syrup, and remaining 4½ cups water.
  4. Stir well, taste, and adjust sweetness if needed.
  5. Serve over ice with lemon slices.

turns.html:
Sparkling Lemonade

A fizzy twist on the classic.

  • 1 cup fresh lemon juice
  • 1 cup granulated sugar
  • 2 cups cold water
  • 2 cups sparkling water or club soda
  • Ice, for serving
  • Lemon slices and mint sprigs, for garnish
  1. Juice the lemons and strain.
  2. Make a simple syrup by warming sugar with 1 cup water until dissolved. Cool.
  3. In a pitcher, mix lemon juice, syrup, and cold water.
  4. Just before serving, add sparkling water and stir gently.
  5. Serve over ice with lemon and mint.

Berry Lemonade

A fruity variation with fresh berries.

  • 1 cup fresh lemon juice
  • 1 cup granulated sugar
  • 4 cups cold water
  • 1 cup fresh raspberries or strawberries, muddled
  • Ice, for serving
  • Lemon slices and berries, for garnish
  1. Juice the lemons and strain.
  2. Make simple syrup with sugar and 1 cup water. Cool.
  3. Muddle berries in a large pitcher. Add lemon juice, syrup, and remaining water.
  4. Stir well and chill for 30 minutes to let flavors meld.
  5. Strain if desired, or serve with berry pieces. Add ice and garnish.

turns.html:
Status Code Remediation Checklist

What to actually do when user_name sees these.

  1. 400 Bad Request — validate the payload schema before retrying.
  2. 401 Unauthorized — refresh the access token, then retry once.
  3. 403 Forbidden — check scopes and resource ownership; don't retry.
  4. 404 Not Found — verify the URL and resource id; may be a stale link.
  5. 409 Conflict — re-read the current state and merge changes.
  6. 429 Too Many Requests — back off exponentially, honour Retry-After.
  7. 500 Internal Server Error — log the trace id, alert the owning service.
  8. 502/504 Gateway — confirm upstream health, then retry with jitter.
  9. 503 Unavailable — queue the work; check autoscaling and circuit breakers.

HTTP Status Codes · Compare

Side-by-side pairings user_name keeps mixing up.

401 vs 403

401 means unauthenticated — no or bad credentials.

403 means authenticated but not permitted.

502 vs 504

502 is a bad response from upstream.

504 is no response in time — a timeout.

301 vs 302

301 is permanent and cacheable.

302 is temporary and shouldn't be cached long.

400 vs 422

400 is malformed syntax.

422 is well-formed but semantically invalid.

Why is my shot sour?
Usually under-extracted. Grind finer in small steps until the shot slows to 25-30s.
Why is my shot bitter?
Over-extracted. Grind coarser, or drop the brew temperature by 1-2°C.
What pressure should I aim for?
9 bar at the group head is the conventional target; some beans taste better at 7-8 bar.
My puck is soggy. Is that bad?
Rarely. It often just means you stopped the shot before the puck dried out.
How much coffee per shot?
Start at 18g in, 36g out for a double, then adjust to taste.

  • ½ cup rolled oats

  • 1 tbsp chia seeds
  • 1 tbsp maple syrup
  • ¼ tsp vanilla extract

Formula
churn = lost / starting_members
Trend
lost members retained
Steps
  1. Pick the period (e.g., May).
  2. Count members at start of month: 1,250.
  3. Count members lost during month: 53.
  4. Divide lost by starting: 53 / 1250 = 4.2%.

A member is lost if their paid subscription cancels or fails to renew during the month and they have no active plan by month-end.

What is the difference between PUT and POST?

PUT replaces the entire resource at a known URI and is idempotent. POST submits data to be processed, often creates a new resource, and is not idempotent.

Everyday Granola

Prep 10 minBake 30 minMakes about 8 cups
Ingredients
  • 3 cups rolled oats
  • 1 cup almonds, chopped
  • 1/2 cup maple syrup
  • 1/3 cup coconut oil, melted
  • 1 tsp vanilla
  • 1/2 tsp salt
  • 1/2 cup dried cranberries
Steps
  1. Heat oven to 325F and line a sheet pan.
  2. Mix oats, almonds, salt in a big bowl.
  3. Whisk syrup, oil, vanilla. Pour over dry.
  4. Spread thin on the pan and bake 25-30 min, stirring halfway.
  5. Cool completely, then fold in cranberries.

turns.html:
Kitchen Composting FAQ

Tap a question to expand. Sources: municipal guidance and master-gardener notes.

What can I put in a kitchen compost bin?
Greens: fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, tea leaves, eggshells. Browns: shredded paper, cardboard, dry leaves. Keep out: dairy, meat, oily food, pet waste.
Why does my bin smell sour?
Usually too wet and too much green material. Add a handful of shredded browns and stir. Aim for a damp-sponge feel, never soggy.
Small flies around the lid — what now?
Fruit flies follow exposed scraps. Bury each addition under 2–3 cm of browns and wipe the rim weekly. A tight lid plus freezing fruit peels first breaks the cycle in about a week.
How long until it's finished?
Indoor countertop bins with worms: 8–12 weeks. Outdoor tumblers: 4–8 weeks in warm weather, longer in winter.

Too much green and not enough air. Add shredded browns (paper, cardboard) to soak moisture, then turn the pile. Layer like lasagna: green, brown, green, brown.

Below 1 m³ a pile rarely heats past 40 °C. Insulate with a ring of straw or move the tumbler to full sun. In winter, expect near-zero microbial activity — that's normal.

Home Coffee Roasting Glossary

  • Green coffee — Raw, unroasted coffee beans.
  • First crack — Audible popping as beans expand and moisture escapes; marks the start of drinkable light roasts.
  • Development time — The period from first crack to the end of the roast; shapes sweetness and body.
  • Roast profile — The planned curve of bean temperature over time.
  • Degassing — Resting roasted beans so CO₂ escapes; usually 1–5 days before brewing.

turns.html:
Home Coffee Roasting Glossary

  • Green coffee — Raw, unroasted coffee beans.
  • First crack — Audible popping as beans expand and moisture escapes; start of drinkable light roasts.

  • Roast profile — Planned curve of bean temperature over time.

  • Drop — Removing beans from the roaster to cool.

  • Second crack — Quieter, faster crackling; signals darker roasts and oils on the surface.

Home Coffee Roasting — Event Order

  1. Charge — Green beans enter the hot roaster. ~0 min
  2. Drying phase — Beans lose surface moisture; green turns yellow. 1–4 min
  3. First crack — Audible popping; start of drinkable light roasts. 5–8 min

  5. Second crack — Quieter crackling; signals darker roasts and surface oils. 9–12 min
  6. Drop — Removing beans to cool. end
  7. Degassing — Resting roasted beans so CO₂ escapes; 1–5 days before brewing. after roast

turns.html:
Lemon Garlic Butter Salmon

Dinner

A quick weeknight salmon with a bright lemon-garlic butter sauce. Serves 2.

Prep10 min
Cook12 min
Calories420 kcal
Ingredients
  • 2 salmon fillets (6 oz each)
  • 3 tbsp unsalted butter
  • 3 cloves garlic, minced
  • 1 lemon, zested and juiced
  • 1 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
  • Salt and pepper to taste
Steps
  1. Pat salmon dry and season both sides with salt and pepper.
  2. Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant.
  3. Place salmon skin-side down and cook 4–5 minutes until the flesh releases easily.
  4. Flip, add lemon juice and zest, and cook 3–4 minutes more.
  5. Spoon sauce over salmon, garnish with parsley, and serve.

turns.html:
Bike-Commute FAQ

Answers to the questions you actually ask on wet mornings, cold starts, and cargo runs.

What should I wear when it rains?
A breathable waterproof shell beats a thick rain jacket. Add fenders if your route has puddles, and tuck trousers into socks or use an ankle strap on the chain side.
How do I keep my chain from rusting?
Wipe and re-lube after every wet ride. A wax-based lube in summer, a wet lube in winter; one drop per roller, then wipe the outside clean.
Is it safe to ride in the dark?
Yes, with lights and reflectivity. A steady front white light, a red rear blinker, and reflective ankle bands are the highest-value upgrades.

conversations.topic: Warehouse order picking accuracy dashboard — formula and steps, branching into layout, filtering, table and chart refinements

turns.html:
Pick Accuracy

Week 32 · Riverside DC · all 6 zones

The formula
pick_accuracy = correct_lines / total_lines
98.4%1,142 correct19 wrong
How we got there
  1. Count every pick line scanned at pack-out.
  2. Flag lines with a wrong SKU, count or damaged unit.
  3. Subtract flagged lines from the total for correct lines.
  4. Divide correct by total, then multiply by 100.

1,142 ÷ 1,161 = 0.9836 → 98.4%

Anything under 98% triggers a zone review the same week.

conversations.topic: Building and refining a watchmaking complications glossary widget

turns.html:
Watchmaking Complications

  • Complication — any function beyond simple hour and minute display.
  • Chronograph — a stopwatch function with start, stop, and reset pushers.
  • Tourbillon — a rotating cage that averages out gravity's effect on the escapement.
  • Perpetual Calendar — automatically tracks date, day, month, leap years until 2100.
  • GMT — a second time zone indicated by an extra 24-hour hand.
  • Power Reserve — how long a wound watch runs before stopping.
  • Minute Repeater — chimes the time on demand with tiny hammers and gongs.

turns.html:
Stovetop Mac & Cheese

Prep 5 minCook 15 minServes 4
one potweeknight
  • 12 oz elbow macaroni
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 2 tbsp all-purpose flour
  • 2 cups whole milk, warm
  • 1 tsp mustard powder
  • 1/2 tsp smoked paprika
  • 8 oz sharp cheddar, shredded
  • 2 oz cream cheese
  • Salt and black pepper, to taste
  1. Boil the pasta in salted water until one minute shy of al dente. Drain, reserving 1/2 cup pasta water.
  2. In the same pot, melt butter over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook 1 minute until it smells nutty.
  3. Stream in warm milk while whisking, then add mustard powder, paprika, salt and pepper. Simmer 3 minutes until it coats a spoon.
  4. Off heat, stir in cheddar and cream cheese a handful at a time until glossy.
  5. Fold in the pasta, loosening with pasta water until it ribbons off the spoon. Serve hot.

Off-heat melting is the trick. Boiling sauce turns cheese grainy.

turns.html:
Picking accuracy

Last week — 3 pick zones, 4 shifts

Formula

accuracy = correct_picks / total_picks

Steps

  1. Audit a random sample of 200 picked lines per shift.
  2. Flag any line with wrong SKU, wrong qty, or wrong batch.
  3. Divide correct lines by total audited lines.
  4. Report per zone and per picker so coaching targets the gap.
Sample size 200 gives ±3.5% margin at 95% confidence — enough to spot drift, not enough to rank pickers by hundredths.

turns.html:
Long-Distance Cycling FAQ

Answers to the questions that come up when you start planning 100 km+ rides, loaded or unloaded.

Typical first long ride 80km comfortably paced
Pannier weight budget 12kg rear only
How far should my first long ride be?
Start at roughly 60–80% of your target distance. If the goal is a century (160 km), build up through 80 km and 120 km rides first. Time on the bike matters more than raw distance — a 4-hour ride at an easy pace teaches you more than a 2-hour hammerfest.
What should I carry in my panniers?
Keep total weight under 12 kg for a rear-only setup. Pack: 2 spare tubes, tyre levers, mini pump, multi-tool, chain lube, 2 litres of water, 1500 kcal of food, lightweight rain jacket, electrolyte tablets. Leave the "just in case" items at home — you can buy almost anything en route.
Front panniers or rear only?
Rear only for loads under 10 kg. Add front panniers when you need more than 12 kg total or when the rear feels unstable on descents. Front low-riders improve handling with heavy loads because they keep the weight low and centred.
How do I pace a long ride?
Aim for a heart rate you could hold for a conversation (zone 2). On a loaded bike, expect 2–4 km/h slower than your unloaded average. Start 10% easier than you think you should, and let the last third of the ride feel like the strongest.
When should I eat and drink?
Eat 60 g of carbohydrate per hour (roughly one banana plus a cereal bar). Drink 500–750 ml per hour in mild weather, more in heat. Set a timer for every 20 minutes until it becomes habit — hunger on a long ride is a planning failure, not a fitness one.
What tyre pressure for a loaded tour?
For 40 mm tyres with 12 kg of luggage, run 45–55 psi rear and 35–45 psi front. Lower pressure improves grip and comfort on rough surfaces; too low risks pinch flats. Check pressure before every long ride — tubeless tyres lose a few psi per week.

Long-Distance Cycling FAQ

Season-aware answers: the same question often has a different answer in July than in January.

Summer tyre pressure 50psi rear, loaded
Winter tyre pressure 38psi rear, loaded
Summer (Jun–Aug): how far should my first long ride be?
Start at 60–80% of your target. In summer heat, start before 7 am or after 5 pm. A 160 km century in July needs 4–5 litres of water and extra electrolytes — plan refill stops every 30 km.
Winter (Dec–Feb): how far should my first long ride be?
Keep distance similar but expect 20–30% slower average speed. Daylight is the real limit — a 100 km winter ride can take 6 hours with stops. Carry lights and a reflective layer even for a day ride.
Summer: what should I carry in my panniers?
Add 1.5 litres of extra water, sunscreen, and a light long-sleeve layer for evening. Total weight still under 12 kg. Sunscreen costs almost nothing in weight and saves your ride the next day.
Winter: what should I carry in my panniers?
Add warm gloves, a spare buff, and a compact emergency blanket. Water bottles freeze — use an insulated bottle or carry water close to your body. Keep total weight under 12 kg; cold-weather kit is denser, not heavier.
How do I pace a long ride in summer?
Start at dawn, take a long midday break in shade, then ride the afternoon. Zone 2 heart rate still applies, but heat raises it by 5–10 bpm at the same effort. Drink before you are thirsty.
How do I pace a long ride in winter?
Warm up slowly — cold muscles need 20 minutes of easy spinning before you push. Keep the first hour strictly zone 1–2. In wind and rain, expect the same effort to produce 4–6 km/h less speed.

60–80% of target. Tarmac lets you hold a steady pace, so a 100 km first ride is reasonable if you have been doing 50 km regularly. Build to 120 km before attempting 160 km.
Gravel: how far should my first long ride be?
Half of your tarmac distance. Gravel is 30–50% slower for the same effort. A 50 km gravel ride is as demanding as an 80 km tarmac ride. Build slowly — the surface punishes overconfidence.
Tarmac: what tyre pressure for a loaded tour?
40 mm tyres: 55 psi rear, 45 psi front with 12 kg luggage. Tarmac allows higher pressure with less penalty. Check before every ride — a 10 psi drop costs you speed and increases puncture risk.
Gravel: what tyre pressure for a loaded tour?
40 mm tyres: 38 psi rear, 30 psi front with 12 kg luggage. Lower pressure lets the tyre conform to the surface and find grip. Go too low and you risk pinch flats on embedded rocks — 30 psi is the practical floor for loaded gravel.
Mixed: how do I pace a long ride?
Plan the tarmac sections as recovery and the gravel as effort. Ride the gravel at zone 2 and the tarmac at zone 2 as well — the point is consistency, not speed. Expect your average speed to be 5–8 km/h lower than a pure tarmac route.
Mixed: what should I carry in my panniers?
Add a spare derailleur hanger and a small brush for mud. Gravel dust works into everything. Keep total weight under 12 kg; the extra mechanical spares are worth the 200 g.

1. How do I pace a long ride?
Aim for a conversational heart rate (zone 2). On a loaded bike expect 2–4 km/h slower than unloaded. Start 10% easier than you think you should; the last third should feel strongest.
2. How far should my first long ride be?
60–80% of your target distance. Build through 80 km and 120 km before attempting a century. Time on the bike matters more than raw distance.
3. What should I carry in my panniers?
Under 12 kg rear-only. Two spare tubes, tyre levers, mini pump, multi-tool, chain lube, 2 litres of water, 1500 kcal of food, light rain jacket, electrolyte tablets. Buy the rest en route.
4. When should I eat and drink?
60 g of carbohydrate per hour. 500–750 ml of water per hour in mild weather. Set a 20-minute timer until it becomes habit. Hunger on a long ride is a planning failure.
5. What tyre pressure for a loaded tour?
40 mm tyres with 12 kg luggage: 45–55 psi rear, 35–45 psi front. Lower pressure improves grip and comfort; too low risks pinch flats. Check before every ride.
6. Front panniers or rear only?
Rear only under 10 kg. Add front panniers above 12 kg or when the rear feels unstable on descents. Front low-riders keep weight low and centred.

turns.html:
Long-Distance Cycling FAQ — Multi-day Trips

The same questions, but for trips with overnight stops.

Daily distance 90km sustainable for most
Recovery rule 1day per 3 ridden
How far should I ride per day on a multi-day trip?
90 km is sustainable for most riders on mixed terrain. Plan a rest day every fourth day or reduce to 60 km on day four. The first day sets the pattern — finish it feeling like you could do it again.
How do I pace a multi-day trip?
Ride the first two hours of every day at zone 1. The cumulative fatigue of a week is the real challenge, not any single day. Keep heart rate capped at zone 2 for the whole trip; the final day should feel the easiest.
How should I manage eating across multiple days?
Eat a proper breakfast, 60 g of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and a real meal in the evening. Post-ride protein within 30 minutes helps recovery. Do not rely on bars alone for more than two days.
What should I carry for a multi-day trip?
Everything from a single long ride plus: a second set of cycling clothes, a small wash kit, a power bank, and a paper map or offline navigation. Total weight 8–12 kg. Launder clothes by hand every second night.
How do I avoid injury on a multi-day trip?
Adjust your position before you leave. The small aches of day one become injuries by day five. Stretch for 10 minutes after every ride. Take a rest day if any pain lasts more than two hours.
What if I get injured mid-trip?
Stop. A rest day costs you one day; riding through an injury can end the trip. Find a train station, reduce the daily distance, or take a full day off. Most multi-day injuries are overuse, not trauma — time is the cure.

turns.html:
Long-Distance Cycling FAQ — Weekly Training Plan

What to do between long rides to build fitness without burning out.

Weekly volume 6h minimum for progress
Long ride 1x per week
How many days a week should I ride?
Three to four rides per week: one long ride, one interval session, and one or two easy recovery rides. Two consecutive rest days are fine and often better than riding tired.
What does a typical training week look like?
Monday rest. Tuesday intervals (4 x 5 minutes at threshold). Wednesday easy 45 minutes. Thursday rest. Friday easy 45 minutes. Saturday long ride. Sunday recovery spin or rest. Total 6–8 hours.
How do I build up to a century?
Add 10% to your long ride each week for three weeks, then take a recovery week at 60% volume. Start at 60 km and build to 120 km over eight weeks. Do not add distance and intensity in the same week.
Should I do intervals if I just want to finish a long ride?
Yes, but keep them short. Four 5-minute efforts at a hard but sustainable pace once a week improve your endurance more than extra easy miles. Skip them entirely in the week before a big ride.
How do I know if I am overtraining?
Resting heart rate up 5+ bpm, poor sleep, no motivation, and heavy legs that do not recover after an easy day. Take three full rest days. Fitness is built during recovery, not during the ride.
What about strength training?
Two 30-minute sessions per week: squats, lunges, and core work. Off-bike strength prevents the back and knee pain that ends long rides early. Do them on rest days, not before the long ride.

conversations.topic: Interactive chocolate chip cookie recipe card with batch scaling, doneness dashboard, and side-by-side butter vs shortening comparison

turns.html:
Brown Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies

Prep 20 minChill 30 minBake 11 minMakes 18
  • 2¼ cups all-purpose flour
  • 1 tsp baking soda
  • 1 tsp fine sea salt
  • 1 cup unsalted butter, browned
  • 1 cup packed dark brown sugar
  • ½ cup granulated sugar
  • 2 large eggs + 1 yolk
  • 2 tsp vanilla extract
  • 2 cups bittersweet chocolate chunks
  • Flaky salt, for finishing
  1. Brown the butter in a light-colored pan until amber and nutty; cool 15 minutes.
  2. Whisk flour, baking soda, and salt in a bowl.
  3. Beat browned butter with both sugars until glossy, 3 minutes.
  4. Add eggs and vanilla; beat until ribbons form.
  5. Fold in dry ingredients, then chocolate chunks. Chill 30 minutes.
  6. Scoop 3-tablespoon mounds onto lined sheets, 2 inches apart.
  7. Bake at 375°F for 10–12 minutes until edges are set and centers look underdone.
  8. Tap the sheet on the counter, sprinkle flaky salt, and rest 5 minutes.

Sailing Knots

  • Bowline — Makes a fixed loop at the end of a line that won't slip under load.
  • Clove Hitch — Quick temporary tie to a post or rail; easy to adjust, easy to spill.
  • Figure-Eight — A stopper knot at the rope's end to keep it from running out through a block.
  • Sheet Bend — Joins two ropes of different thickness; holds best when both ends are on the same side.
  • Rolling Hitch — Grips a spar or another line so you can take tension along a rope.

turns.html:
Pancakes · recipe card
Buttermilk pancakes Serves 4 20 min · easy
Prep 10 m Cook 10 m Vege option

Ingredients

  • 250 g plain flour
  • 2 tbsp caster sugar
  • 1 tsp baking powder
  • 1 pinch salt
  • 300 ml buttermilk
  • 1 large egg
  • 2 tbsp melted butter
  • Oil for the pan

Method

  1. Whisk flour, sugar, baking powder and salt in a large bowl.
  2. Crack in the egg, pour the buttermilk and melted butter. Stir until just combined — lumps are fine.
  3. Rest the batter 10 minutes while the pan heats on medium.
  4. Ladle a small pour into a lightly oiled pan. Flip when bubbles pop on the surface, about 2 minutes.
  5. Cook 1 minute more, stack and keep warm while you finish the rest.

Audience reach by channel overlap

Estimate unique people reached by Instagram and YouTube when some viewers see both.

reach = |IG| + |YT| - |IG ∩ YT|
  1. Count Instagram viewers: 1,200.
  2. Count YouTube viewers: 800.
  3. Count people who saw both: 300.
  4. Apply inclusion–exclusion: 1,200 + 800 − 300 = 1,700.

Result: 1,700 unique people.

This avoids double-counting the overlap.

turns.html:
Sourdough FAQ

Answers to the questions that come up most in a home kitchen.

My starter isn't rising — what's wrong?
Usually temperature. Below 21 °C a starter can look dead for days. Move it somewhere warm and feed it twice a day for three days before judging.
How wet should the dough be?
Most beginner recipes sit around 70–75% hydration. Higher hydration gives an open crumb but is much harder to shape.
Why is my crumb dense and gummy?
Usually under-fermentation or slicing too soon. Let the loaf cool fully — at least two hours — before cutting.
Can I keep it in the fridge overnight?
Yes. A cold retard slows fermentation and deepens flavour. Twelve to eighteen hours is the sweet spot.

conversations.topic: Flashcards: computer networks and the OSI model

turns.html:
What is the OSI model?
A 7-layer framework (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) that standardizes how network systems communicate.
Show all 7 layers
  1. Physical — bits over the wire
  2. Data Link — frames on a local link
  3. Network — packets, routing (IP)
  4. Transport — end-to-end segments (TCP/UDP)
  5. Session — dialogue control
  6. Presentation — encoding, encryption
  7. Application — HTTP, DNS, SMTP

turns.html:
Transport layer (L4)
Provides end-to-end delivery between processes. TCP = reliable, ordered, connection-oriented. UDP = best-effort, connectionless, low overhead.
Network layer (L3)
Moves packets between hosts across networks. IP handles addressing and routing; ICMP reports errors.
Data Link layer (L2)
Frames data on the local link. Uses MAC addresses; Ethernet and Wi-Fi live here.

conversations.topic: Building and refining a freediving training glossary widget

turns.html:
Freediving glossary

Terms for breath-hold and depth training.

  • CO₂ tolerance — ability to hold breath with rising carbon dioxide.
  • Static apnea (STA) — breath-hold floating face-down, timed.
  • Dynamic apnea (DYN) — horizontal swim on one breath.
  • Free immersion (FIM) — descending by pulling the rope.
  • Constant weight (CWT) — finning down and up with the same weight.
  • MDR — mammalian dive reflex: bradycardia and blood shift.
  • Samba — loss of motor control after a breath-hold.
  • BO — blackout, loss of consciousness underwater.

turns.html:
Freediving glossary — training & safety

Expanded with training and safety terms.

  • CO₂ tolerance — ability to hold breath with rising carbon dioxide; trained via CO₂ tables.
  • O₂ tolerance — ability to keep clear while oxygen drops; trained via O₂ tables.
  • Static apnea (STA) — breath-hold floating face-down, timed.
  • Dynamic apnea (DYN) — horizontal swim on one breath.
  • Dynamic no-fins (DNF) — horizontal swim without fins.
  • Free immersion (FIM) — descending by pulling the rope.
  • Constant weight (CWT) — finning down and up with the same weight.
  • Variable weight (VWT) — using a weighted sled to descend.
  • No-limits (NLT) — sled down, lift up; competition discontinued.
  • MDR — mammalian dive reflex: bradycardia and blood shift.
  • Blood shift — blood moves into the chest cavity under pressure.
  • Lung squeeze — chest compression at depth.
  • Mouthfill — topping up mouth air from lungs before descent.
  • Frenzel — equalisation technique using tongue as a piston.
  • Valsalva — equalisation by forced exhalation; less used in depth.
  • BTV — voluntary opening of the eustachian tubes.
  • Samba — loss of motor control after a breath-hold.
  • BO — blackout, loss of consciousness underwater.
  • LMC — loss of motor control (samba).
  • Safety diver — trained dive partner who monitors and rescues.

Progressive steps for the first 12 weeks

  1. Week 1–2: Name recognition & eye contact
  2. Week 3–4: Sit & stay (short durations)
  3. Week 5–6: Leash manners & loose-leash walking
  4. Week 7–8: Recall in low-distraction settings
  5. Week 9–10: Crate comfort & alone time
  6. Week 11–12: Doorbell & polite greetings
Short, positive sessions — 5 minutes, three times a day.

conversations.topic: Branched beekeeping FAQ dashboard for <regex>user_name</regex>, refined from a swarm-and-harvest Q&A into a season-aware, sortable, hive-aware widget

turns.html:
Beekeeping FAQ

Four hives, one backyard. Tap a question for the short answer.

Why are my bees bearded on the front of the hive?

Bearding on a warm evening is normal — the colony is hanging outside to dump heat and keep the brood nest near 35 °C. It's only a problem if the entrance is blocked, the lid has no vent, or you smell fermenting honey.

  • Add a screened inner cover or prop the lid 3 mm.
  • Shade the hive after 14:00 in a heatwave.
  • If they beard at dawn instead, suspect varroa or a queenless colony.
When do I add a honey super?

When the brood box has 7–8 of 10 frames drawn and the nectar flow is on. Here that's roughly the last week of May and again after the July dearth breaks.

How much honey can I take?

Leave them 15–20 kg of stores for winter in our climate. Anything above that is yours.

My bees swarmed — did I do something wrong?

Probably not. Swarming is reproduction, not failure. Check for queen cells, cull all but the best two, and the colony will usually requeen itself in three weeks.

Should I treat for varroa?

Yes, if a sugar roll shows more than 3 mites per 100 bees. Treat after the honey harvest, when the colony has no supers on.

turns.html:
Beekeeping FAQ

Swarm control, in the order you actually do it.

A colony that has already swarmed still has a job for you: check cells, then wait.
  1. Open and count queen cells. If you see 8–15, they mean business.
  2. Cull to two. Leave the two best-shaped cells, both on different frames.
  3. Close up for 21 days. No peeking — the virgin queens need quiet.
  4. Check for eggs at day 21. Eggs prove the new queen is laying.
  5. If no eggs, add a frame of brood. A second chance to requeen.
What if they swarm again in the same season?

Uncommon but possible. Split the colony and give each half open brood. Two smaller colonies beat one that keeps issuing casts.

How do I know the new queen mated?

Look for eggs and young larvae in a tight pattern. A mated queen also returns with a slightly darker, fuller abdomen.

Do I need to feed them while they requeen?

Light 1:1 syrup if the flow has stopped, just enough to keep them drawing. Don't overfeed — you'll backfill the brood nest.

Should I mark the new queen?

Yes, in the season's colour. It makes every later inspection faster.

turns.html:
Beekeeping FAQ

One question, expanded: why they beard.

Umi

Bearding is heat management. The colony pushes surplus bees out of the entrance to increase airflow over the brood nest.

Reading it: the brood nest stays near 35 °C until the outside air passes roughly 30 °C, then the bees have to work hard — that's when you see the beard.
What can I do?

Shade, ventilate, and don't open the hive mid-afternoon.

Is bearding a sign of swarming?

No. Swarming bees leave in a cloud and don't return. Bearding bees come home at dusk.

turns.html:
Newsletter list growth — compounding at 3.2% / mo

Six months of subscriber movement, net of unsubscribes.

Compound growth rate
g = (end / start)^(1 / n) - 1
  1. Take starting count 1,000 and ending count 1,212.
  2. Divide: 1,212 ÷ 1,000 = 1.212.
  3. Take the 6th root: 1.212^(1/6) = 1.0325.
  4. Subtract 1 → 0.0325 = 3.25% per month.

  • Discard — The portion of starter removed before feeding to control acidity and volume.

cache

What is a cache line (cache block)?

Tap to reveal the definition.

The smallest unit of data transferred between main memory and the CPU cache. Typical modern size: 64 bytes. The CPU fetches a whole line even if it needs only one byte, because of spatial locality.

card 1

What is a cache line?

Tap to reveal.

Smallest unit of data transferred between main memory and cache. Typically 64 bytes; fetched whole due to spatial locality.

card 2

What does cache associativity mean?

Tap to reveal.

The number of locations in a set where a given memory block may be stored. Direct-mapped = 1 way, N-way set associative = N choices per set, fully associative = anywhere in cache. More ways → fewer conflict misses, but slower lookup and more hardware.

Q: What is a cache line?

card 3

What is a write policy?

Tap to reveal.

How the cache handles writes. Write-through: update memory immediately — simple, safe, slow. Write-back: update memory only when the line is evicted — faster, needs a dirty bit, more complex. Most modern caches are write-back.

card 4

How does a direct-mapped cache work?

Tap to reveal.

Each memory block maps to exactly one cache slot — index = (block address) mod (number of cache slots). Fast and cheap, but two blocks sharing an index conflict: loading one evicts the other even if the rest of the cache is empty.
